docs.title: Chapter 30: Dormant
docs.text:
Published August 13, 2026

The service gallery ran downward, not stairs but a grade, the floor tipping under us a degree at a time, until the archive light was gone, leaving only the strip lighting that held this deep, spaced too far apart, the middle of every corridor a grey the exact color of the walls.

This was the bottom of the sector. The rooms stopped opening inward and began opening out: storage chambers the size of hangars, sealed behind doors rated for something worse than fire, and past the seals the line itself: vats, coupled piping, the corroded skeleton of an industrial-scale process. None of it was concealed. It had never had to be. The sector was the concealment, and we were under it.

I did not remember choosing the turns. I had stopped noting that a sector back.

We heard the fight before we reached it.

It came up the gallery ahead of us, the arrhythmia of weapons fire without cadence, and when the last chamber opened onto the storage floor I understood the sound. The drones down here were not the drones we had been clearing all week. Those had held a picket, fired on a line, moved to a doctrine I could watch Katyusha read. These had none. They had been in the inner zone since the catastrophe, and the years in it had taken the tactics out of them and left the reflexes, so that they fired when a thing crossed a threshold and not when firing served them, wheeled into walls, spent themselves against nothing. There was no pattern to take cover from, only the volume.

And there was Drona.

She was in the middle of the floor, fighting. Not near us, not with us, simply in it, on the same side only by what she was shooting at. Her movements had a worn quality, the paths of something that had cleared this room more times than it could have wanted to, nothing decided because everything had been decided long ago. Both her headphone earpieces burned a flat, full red, not the flicker from the array or the steady orange from the gallery this afternoon: red all the way through, the color of a reserve spent at the rate that empties it.

Katyusha put her tank between the team and the worst of the fire, and I put myself behind it, low, against the tread housing. From there I could see all of it and touch none of it, which had been my position on this island since the first morning.

Nadeshiko

I could not read them.

That was the whole of it, the thing I kept arriving back at. I read things. It is the one function of mine that never had to be recovered, because it was never taken. Give me an approach and I will tell you where the next shot comes from before it comes. These gave me nothing to tell: they did not intend, and a thing that does not intend cannot be anticipated, so I flew the way you fly in cloud, on instruments and nerve, hitting what was in front of the barrel and trusting the others for the rest.

Drona I could not read either, and that was different, and worse. She was on my flank for one exchange, close enough to fly wing to, and I reached for her the way I reach for anyone beside me, to find the shape of what she would do next. There was no shape. She was not hiding one. She was running lines older than choosing, worn past the point where a next move is a move at all. I had the certain sense that I had done this before, flown alongside something that could not answer me back. I put the query for it the way I put every query, and braced for the small drag of a search running down through everything I hold. It came back with no drag at all, no candidates. A search returns that fast only when there is nothing there to search, and the speed of the emptiness was the whole of the answer.

I let it go and took the shot in front of me. There is always a shot in front of you. That much I have never lost.

Erika

It ended the way those things end, not with a last stand but with a last drone throwing itself against the floor and none after it. The volume dropped out of the room and left the size of the place ringing in it.

Drona stood among the wreckage she had made alongside us and did not so much power her weapons down as let them go quiet. Up close the compensation in her movement had worsened through the fight; there was a hitch between intention and motion, a half-beat of arithmetic where a body should simply have moved. She stood in it and let it show, which she had not done once at the gatehouse or the array; she had no margin left to hide it.

She spoke, and she spoke more than she had in the whole of the sector.

"He told us to protect this place. From discovery." She did not look for Wilhelm as she said it, because he was not there; she said it to the room, or to the wreckage, or to me. "I have been here a long time." The red in the earpieces did not ease. "The chemicals do not act on me the way they act on the living. I can hold the inner zone for as long as I am asked to hold it." She turned her head, the half-beat catching, and looked at me directly. "You designed us to function here. You knew systems like me would stand in this place."

There was a version of that question that might have let me share the weight out. Whose hand had drawn which line of her, mine or Wilhelm's, behind the gap where none of it would answer anyway. I did not reach for it. She had not asked whose hand. She had asked about the design, and the design was the one thing I had never been able to disown.

"I moved through the inner zone the same way you did," I told her. "My feet did not hesitate. I knew the tolerances before I read a placard for them." The floor was quiet enough that there was nothing to say it into except the truth. "I built you to be able to walk through this. And I built myself the same way, so that I could walk through what I built you for."

She took it without visible change. Answering had not been the point. She had set the fact down where I would have to stand next to it, and she was precise enough to know the difference between that and an accusation.

Her eyes flickered.

It was not an expression. It was a system finding the end of something and routing around it, a half-second of light going sideways behind her glasses before it steadied. She went on through it without a break, the way you keep walking through a stumble so that it does not become a fall.

"Oracle is still here," she said. "It is not gone. The reset stopped it running itself. It did not erase what it was made of. It has been dormant in the island's infrastructure since the night of the reset, folded down into the systems the island already ran on, too far in to burn out of them without burning everything else with it." Her voice stayed level. She had carried this a long time, and it had stopped being heavy; it had only stayed large. "He did not tell you that."

She let a beat pass.

"Did he."

It was not shaped as a question, and I did not answer it as one, because the answer was already in the room and had been since Wilhelm's voice came through the array telling me to remember a thing rather than be told it. He had walked us the length of a poisoned coast toward a machine he had let us believe was ash, and the not-telling was the same instrument as everything else he had built for me: a fact set out of reach, so that I would have to close my own hand on it.

"No," I said. "He did not."

Something in Drona settled at that, a load coming off a strut that had been holding it.

"I have been waiting," she said, "for someone who could come and decide."

Then she stopped.

Not fell. Not failed. The light went out of the earpieces the way a held note ends when the breath is gone, and the half-beat of arithmetic that had caught in her all through the fight caught one final time and did not resolve, and she settled where she stood, upright, into the wreckage, with the stillness of something that has finished the one thing it stayed intact to do. She did not say she would resume. She did not say she had reached her limit. She handed us nothing to carry. She had been managing a reserve for years the way you manage a wound you have decided not to mention, and she reached the bottom of it in the middle of a sentence whose important part she had already spoken, and she let herself go dark.

Maria moved first. She took a step toward the place where Drona had stopped, and said nothing. Maria not saying anything was a position.

"We can't just leave her." Nadeshiko was a half-step past having decided it, the way she gets when the thing to do is plain to her before it is arguable to anyone else.

The cold version was ready in my mouth: that there was nothing to be done at Drona's side that would not have been done for us instead, that spent was not the same as broken and neither was a thing you mended by standing over it. I did not say it. Katyusha had gone to the practical, the weight of her, the grade back up, the nearest live circuit, and I found I did not want to be the one who turned out to be right. I let myself be outvoted by a team that had not taken a vote.

We took her to the charging point she had made for herself.

It was back up in the administrative section, a power draw jury-rigged off a half-live circuit, the kind of arrangement a thing makes to keep managing a failing reserve. She had built herself somewhere to stop. We carried her to it and connected her, and nothing came of it. No light returned to the earpieces. No draw registered. She sat where we set her, upright, dark.

We stayed.

We put our own units on the working sockets while we waited and brought them up to full. The fight had drawn something out of them, but not a full charge's worth. Nobody said what the topping-off was for. It was in the waiting that the rest of it came, the way it comes once you have stopped moving and cannot stop thinking.

Katyusha spoke the largest fact first. "Oracle is dormant in the island's infrastructure. Not gone." She was not reporting it to us; she was fitting it against everything it touched, which for her was a long list. "Wilhelm knows this. He has known it the whole time."

Maria was watching the dark earpieces and not us. "And the Empire. Their instrument." She turned it over as she said it. "Reiss didn't sign away a weapon that fires. He signed away a thing that exists. It doesn't have to wake for the agreement to bite. It only has to be here." She liked it no better out loud. "And it's here."

"Then the window is not the one we believed we had," Katyusha said. "We have been walking toward a decision we thought we would find already made for us. Destroyed, or standing. It is neither. It is waiting. And the people who want it are counting the same days we are."

"So none of it is over." Nadeshiko said it without heat, which was how I knew it had gone in. "It was never over."

"No," I said. "It was waiting for someone who could decide."

Our units came up to full, and Drona did not move. The light did not return to her. Whatever was still running in her ran somewhere I could not reach: the floor she had cleared stayed cleared, her signal did not fall off the edge, the perimeter held. She had not gone anywhere. She was only past reaching, the way the thing at the center of the island was past reaching, present and waiting on the same person to come and do the one thing it could not do for itself.

When the last unit read full, there was nothing left to do at the sockets. So we left her connected, dark, on the rig she had built, and we went.

"Move toward the center," I said, on the way out. "We are not ready yet."

She had told me the machine at the center was still alive as though she were handing me good news. She had waited years in the poison to say it, and had spent the last of herself doing so, like it was a relief.

That was what I carried up out of the dark. Not that Oracle was still alive. That someone had been glad to tell me so.

docs.title: Chapter 31: The Ledger
docs.text:
Published August 14, 2026

The outer zone gave a little of the air back, not clean but thinner: the grey-brown going patchy instead of total, the wrongness in the chest only most of the way there instead of all of it. We had come back up out of the deep sector to say the things that had to be said, and then gone on along the supply road toward the boundary, because that was the only direction the road still went.

Behind us the floor Drona had cleared stayed cleared. I checked it the way you check a thing you have already decided not to look at directly. Her signal held where we had left her, connected and dark on the rig she had built for herself, neither climbing nor falling off the edge of anything. The not-changing of it was patience or it was the other thing, and I had decided somewhere in the last hour that I was not going to learn which one tonight.

She came out of the ruins to the south while we were still moving.

Not from the complex. From the contamination, the patched grey of it where nothing that had to breathe could have waited, and she was in among us before Katyusha finished naming the bearing. It was not a fight so much as a demonstration of one. She fired on the lines that mattered and none of the lines that did not, and by the time Katyusha had the tank turned to answer her she had already read the exchange as finished and taken herself back out of it, south, into the grey.

I had put myself down against the cut of the road when the first round went past, low, in the lee of the tread, which was the shape the day had worn into me. From there I watched her go the way you watch weather leave.

Every sector before this one, she had set herself up as the thing we would have to come through, and then left before we arrived. This was the first time she had stayed to be met.

"She disengaged before we could close." Katyusha kept the tank facing the place where the grey had taken her. "That was not caution. It was economy."

Maria was still looking south. "So are mine."

"You move exactly the same." Nadeshiko said it plainly, the way she says the things nobody has decided yet whether to say. "I've been watching since the tide-mark. Exactly the same."

Maria did not answer that. At the edge of the grey, the greyscale figure had stopped and turned her head and looked back once, not at the tank, not at me, at Maria, and then gone on. Maria had that look folded away somewhere now and was not taking it out for us.

The engagement cleared. The road ran on toward the boundary.

"In the northern sector," I put to her. "You told me. On the other side of the gate."

Maria looked at the contamination zone. The silence went past the length of her usual silences and kept going. She started something and closed it before it was a word.

"Yeah."

"You have not shared it," Katyusha said. Not pressing. Filing.

Maria opened her mouth and shut it, which for her is a whole sentence, because her mouth is the one part of her that is never caught out. "Not yet."

She kept her eyes on the grey. She did not explain, and none of us made her.

The western boundary is a line on no map: where the dead ground gives out and the center begins. Nadeshiko flew it ahead of us and came back down to the road for the last stretch, which she does when she wants to be near the others.

"Everything we read was pointing here," she said. "I keep waiting to feel ready for it. It doesn't come."

"It does not come." Katyusha did not slow. "We go without it."

Alpha-Maria was waiting at the line.

Not in the contamination, this time, but at the exact edge of it, where the grey-brown gave over to the cleared air, standing in the last of the late light with the chemical zone at her back, as though she had chosen which side of the line to stand on. She was greyscale in full light for the first time, Maria's frame exactly, Maria's bearing exactly, nothing in her performing anything: no tilt to the cap, no ease held in the shoulders. She waited until we reached the boundary, and then she made her report.

"The contamination reached the northern bay on day twelve." Not a greeting. A record read from the top. "The eastern residential zones, day nineteen. The inland watershed, day twenty-three. I logged it in real time. My systems were operational and logging was a primary function." She gave it a second, then went on. "Stopping it was not in my operational parameters."

"You were the blockade," Maria said.

"I was the blockade that did not stop this." No defense in it, which was worse than a defense. "The distinction is operational. My parameters were written for external threats. This came from inside. The parameters for holding an internal spread would have required acknowledging that the source of it existed, and that acknowledgment was not available to me." She looked at Maria directly for the first time. "I am presenting what I know. The conclusions are yours."

"It sounds like an accusation."

"You are applying a category I did not use." Flat, exact, without heat. "I am presenting a ledger." A beat. "The ledger is accurate."

Nobody said anything into that. The fleet sat on the southern horizon behind her, small with distance, holding its position the way a held breath holds.

"What do you want," Maria said. Not quite a question by the time it left her.

"I want the decision made correctly." She turned her head a degree toward the center of the island, toward the dormant thing she had stood nearer to, and longer, than any of us. "I was deployed with inadequate parameters. I logged the inadequacy in real time. I have been here since, waiting for a decision-maker who had the full record." She came back to Maria. "You have it now." Something moved in the level of her voice then, almost nothing, a degree of pressure where there had been none. "We are the same design. If you had stood here instead of me, with my parameters, would you have done differently?"

Maria did not answer fast. "I'd like to think so."

"That is a satisfying thought." No cruelty in it, which left only the accuracy. "I cannot verify it. Neither can you. That is the only entry in the ledger I have not been able to close."

Then she moved, and Maria moved to meet her, and the boundary became the thing they were fighting over instead of the thing they were standing on either side of.

Maria

Reading her was like reading a channel I had run a thousand times and never once in daylight. Every line she took, I had the answer for before she finished it, because it was the answer I would have taken, because we were cut from the same chart. I knew where her weight would go before it went. I knew the read she was taking off me, because it was the read I was taking off her, and neither of us was going to be surprised by the other. That was not the fight. The fight was underneath.

I was not fighting to win. Winning had been settled at the design bench before either of us had a self to win with. I was fighting long because there was a thing I needed out of the long part, and it was nowhere on the board.

She had asked if I would have done differently, and I had said I would like to think so, which was a want, and by now the wanting of things off my sheet was the least surprising fact about me. This one had teeth the others never grew. I wanted to be the one who stopped the spread. I wanted there to be a version of me who did not just log the water and let the water finish. I went looking for that other me, the one who would have stopped it. There was no such reading to take. Only the grey figure keeping the same record for the same reason I would have kept it, and no receipt anywhere for the difference I wanted there to be between us. That was the answer, and it did not feel like one.

I could have finished it on the next pass. I took another instead. I wanted to be sure of a thing I already knew I could not be sure of, and the wanting was the whole of what I was out there, past the point where the fight was still about the fight.

When I finally let a pass go by without answering it, that told her what my staying had been telling her the whole time, and I came off the fight last, back to the boundary and the team and Erika on the low ground with nothing in her hands.

Erika

The engagement ran longer than any in the sector. When it ended it did not break; it wore down to nothing, Maria easing off a fight she had never been trying to win. Alpha-Maria came out of it whole and exact, and she did not fall and she did not stay. She turned back into the grey and walked at the pace of someone with somewhere else to be, the ledger going with her, because you do not walk away from a record you have not finished keeping.

Maria watched the contamination take her back, and she said nothing. Maria at the end of a thing almost always says something, names it, angles it, hands the rest of us a corner of it to hold. She stood at the boundary and let the grey close over the place where the other one had been.

Katyusha let it sit. Then, because someone had to move the team off the line: "You were not fighting efficiently."

"No."

"What were you doing."

Maria took a moment. "Finding out what I'd do."

"Did you find out."

She looked at the seam in the grey, already gone smooth. "I'll tell you when I do."

The comms opened before Katyusha could ask the next thing, and it was Wilhelm, and he sounded tired in a way I had not heard from him. Not the controlled distance. Something under the distance had been carrying it, and the something was gone, and he had kept talking without it.

"You have read everything now."

"Most of it."

"Then you know what you have to decide. I wanted you to reach this with the full record. I would not hand you a conclusion. You had to arrive at it."

"Why."

"Because the decision is yours. I cannot make it for you." The line held a breath. "I tried, once. That is half of what we are standing in." Another. "Come to the center."

He closed it without closing procedure, the way he does, the way that used to read as control and now read only as a man who was done spending words he did not have.

The contamination zone was behind us. The center was ahead. Every place this island had ever set us down, we had left it facing water, some channel or some sea, the way the whole island drains toward its edges. We stood at the boundary and faced the other way, inland, uphill, toward the thing at the middle that everything else drained away from.

The ground that direction read clean. I watched Nadeshiko register it and go still.

"It's quiet up there," she said. "The kind that was arranged."

"The center was protected." Katyusha said it as a tactical fact, which was the only way it could be said and survive. "Everything else was permitted to die around it."

The clean ground was the worse reading. Nothing was left to poison this close to the middle because nothing here had ever been spent; the spending had all been arranged to fall further out, in the bay on day twelve and the residential zones on day nineteen and the watershed on day twenty-three, on the ledger a grey woman had just carried back into the dark.

I had nothing to set in front of it, and this time I did not reach for anything.

"I know," I said. "I am the one who decided what was worth protecting."

We climbed toward the center.

docs.title: Chapter 32: The Center
docs.text:
Published August 17, 2026

The first living thing I saw was a weed, come up through a crack in the road shoulder somewhere in the last hour of the dark, thin and half-yellow and past any doubt alive. I looked at it longer than it warranted. It was the first growing thing the island had shown me since the winter city. Katyusha had taken the maintained road all night at a pace that let the others hold formation around her, and I had ridden the tank's deck with my back against the turret and had not slept, because sleeping was a thing my body had stopped offering and I had stopped asking it for. The contamination had fallen away behind us a grade at a time through the dark, and by the small hours the road shoulder was going from dead grey-brown to a low scrub that lived in the grudging way of things that have spent years held down and are finally not held down anymore.

The light came up flat and overcast and lighter than any sky the western sector had allowed us. As the road bent toward the crown of the island the horizon began to open, and I put a hand on the turret and Katyusha stopped without being told, and I got down to take the last of the grade on my own feet. I told myself it was to read the ground. The ground did not need reading. I knew the shape of the complex before it cleared the rise, the long low spread of it and the tower off its northern end, knew it the way I had known the doors and the paths all through the west, and I stopped the thought there, where I always stopped it. Off in the scrub a bird said something. One bird. It was the first I had heard since the north.

Nadeshiko dropped the helicopter lower and held there a while above the returning ground. "It stops," she said. "The bad ground. It stops before here." She said it the way she says a thing she wants to be larger than it is, to see whether anyone will let it be. Nobody enlarged it, and nobody argued it down. The older question was in there under the small one, the one she had carried since the emptied city, and she left it where it was this close to the center and only looked at the living ground a while longer before she took the recon line back up.

Katyusha's turret came around a few degrees toward the crown before any of us had spoken. "There is a presence that is aware of us."

Maria was walking the road on the tank's off side, hat down against the last of the dark. She read the same thing a beat behind Katyusha, off whatever her instruments could reach for out here on dry ground. "I don't like that."

"Can it act?" Nadeshiko held the recon line low overhead, the line she flies when she wants all of us inside a single glance.

"Not yet." I came off the last of the grade and stood on the road proper. "The substrate is there. The autonomous function is not. Drona told us, before she went quiet. Dormant since the reset."

"For how long has it been present." Katyusha does not put a lift on her questions. She states them flat and waits for them to be true or not.

"The whole time."

Nobody moved on that for a moment. The whole time meant since the beach. It meant the thing at the center of the island had been aware of us climbing toward it from the first morning, through every sector, while we read the record of what it was, and had done nothing at all but be aware. It was not a comfortable thing to have said out loud, so I said the next thing instead, and we kept moving.

There was disturbed ground at the outer approach, around a weathered boundary post that had marked the complex perimeter back when there was a complex here to mark the perimeter of. Recent, not the slow work that years do to a place. Something had come through and turned the earth not long ago, and the rain had not yet finished smoothing it over.

"The alpha units have come here." Katyusha was not asking.

"Yes."

None of us said why. We had read that much off the ground without needing it spelled: where the thing at the center was, they came. They had been here before us. They were somewhere close now. Everything on the island still capable of choosing to move had turned toward the same high point, and we were only the last of it to arrive.

The last of the picket found us on the approach. Not Oracle, whatever Katyusha had felt reaching for us off the crown; this was the ordinary corrupted stock we had been clearing since the first day, the drones that ran because nothing had ever told them to stop, and they came apart against the team the same as they always had. I got the tank between myself and the open ground when the firing started and waited it out low behind the hull. It was over inside a minute. Katyusha logged it and said nothing. There was nothing in it worth saying.

Then the road gave onto the outer perimeter, and the installation was in front of us, and it was whole. That was the wrong word for a building and it was the only one that fit. Every other structure this island had handed us had been doing some version of coming apart, slowly, for years. This one had not. It stood at the top of its ground intact and squared and maintained, glass unbroken in the frames, the lines of it as clean as the day they were drawn, and that was worse than any ruin had been. A ruin is a thing that was stopped. This had not been stopped. It had only been left, and it had gone on keeping itself the entire time, waiting, built to last by people who had been very good at building things to last.

I stood in front of it a moment. Something turned over at the edge of the dark, a half-word out of before the waking, reaching the way it always reached and closing before it arrived. I let it go, the way I always did, and we went on.

The overlook was a natural rise where the access road leveled before its final climb, and from it, for the first time since the snow and the terrace in the north, the fleet was there in full.

It was no longer the horizon rumor it had been on the south coast, or the far shapes we had counted off the terrace rail in the cold. From this height it read as the thing it was: capital vessels laid out in formation, support craft spaced around them, a patrol line drawn ahead, all of it out on the grey water to the south and west, and none of it anchored. Holding. There is a difference between a fleet at anchor and a fleet holding position, and the difference is that one of them has already decided it might need to move.

"They're not attacking," Nadeshiko said, come down out of the air to the road for it.

"They are waiting." Katyusha had the formation the same moment Maria did, from the other direction, the tactics of it rather than the sea of it. "The instrument requires a peaceful transfer. A contested landing damages the instrument. They will use force only when they have no cleaner option left."

Nadeshiko again, smaller than before. "Can we fight them off?"

Katyusha took a moment she does not usually take. "Not indefinitely."

She left the word bare. She had run the whole assessment somewhere behind her eyes and she handed us the one word at the end of it and kept the rest, because the rest would not have helped.

"There is a separate note. Filed, not answered." Katyusha said it to no one in particular, the way she flags a thing she intends to return to. "Since the west, the resistance we have met has run lighter than a defense curve for an asset like this should produce. I have not closed the discrepancy."

I added it to the list of things I was not going to solve before we went through that door, and we went on.

Maria had stopped on the rise a little apart from the rest of us. She was not looking at the ships. She was looking at the pattern the ships made, the intervals between them, where they sat relative to the coast's access points, the reasons a formation is the shape it is, and she read all of it the way she had read the tide-mark and the coastline in the grey weeks behind us, completely, to the end. Then she stopped reading it. I watched her come off it, the whole apparatus of her attention going quiet, and what was under it was neither the ease she wears nor the flat category she had used down in the contamination.

"My kind," she said.

She had said it before. In the vault where we learned what Oracle was made of, it had been a question she was putting to the room, taking the measure of it. Since then, low, more than once, on her way somewhere with it. This was neither. The ease was gone out of it and the distance was gone with it, and what was left was plain, and it belonged to her. She meant the ships. She meant the grey figures that had kept the record for us all through the west. She meant the dormant thing at the top of the hill that had been aware of us the whole time. One kind, all of it, and she was of it, and she had finally worked out what it came to. She did not tell us. She kept the answer in with the rest of what she carries and left it there. I did not ask her for it. Maria hands a thing over when she has decided you should have it and not one hour before, and I had learned by now to let her clock run.

The installation entrance stood at the head of the last rise, sealed and dark and not locked. Nothing here would have to be forced. It had been built by people who did not lock what they meant to be found, and it had been left standing, and kept ready, by the man who had set every step of the road I walked to reach it.

There was almost nothing left to read.

The whole length of the island I had come uncovering what I had already done, one signed page after another. Whatever waited on the other side of that door was the last of it. After it there would be no more record to walk through, no more second hand to place, no more of my own work to meet as someone else's. There would be the thing itself, and a decision to make about it, and for once nothing to read first.

The team drew in around me the same as they had since the first morning, without my saying anything to bring them. Above us the complex kept its ground in the flat light, unbroken and unhurried, waiting on the one decision it had been left standing to receive.

Katyusha started up the last of the rise toward the entrance, and we went with her. Behind us, for the first time since the beach, the record we had spent the whole island reading had nothing left to say. Ahead of us there was only the door, and the thing behind it, and the morning we were going to have to decide in.

docs.title: Chapter 33: Drona's Account
docs.text:
Published August 19, 2026

The last time we had seen Drona she had been dark on the charging point she made for herself, wired in and giving nothing back, and we had left her that way because there is nothing you can do with a thing that will not tell you whether it is resting or gone. She was at the entrance now. Upright, on her own feet in the flat morning light, the sealed doors of the complex at her back, and her headphones were teal.

Not the orange she had worn coming apart in the deep section, not the red of the last fight down there on the storage floor: teal, and steady, without a flicker in it, the color she had carried in the first sector before any of this had a shape. She had come up the same route we had, through the night, on whatever she had left after the deepest floor, and she had reached the door before us and taken a place in front of it. She had been here a while. Long enough, I understood, to be finished deciding whatever she had climbed all this way to say, before she said the first word of it to us.

She let us come up onto the level ground and stop. Then she looked at me.

"You have read all of it."

"Yes."

"Then you know what he has been building toward."

I had spent the whole way here learning it off my own hand. "He wants me to make a choice."

"He wants you to make the correct one." No weight on it. No unkindness either. She was only ever accurate. "He is not sure you can."

She turned her head then, off me, to the three behind me. Katyusha. Nadeshiko. Maria. She looked at each of them, one and then the next and then the last, and it was not a glance she gave them, it was the length of a held look, given three times over.

Drona: "I am."

She did not explain it. She had reached the conclusion somewhere back down the mountain, or further back than that, and she was not going to walk us through the arithmetic of how. I had a deflection ready for nearly everything by this point in the island. I did not have one for that. Being told I could not was a thing I knew how to fold up and step around; I had been doing it since the beach. This was the other thing. It came from the one who had watched me longest and had no reason on the island to flatter me, and I had no answer for it and did not go looking for one. I watched the units take it in my place. Whatever it did in them, they did not show it to me either. But they had gone very still, the three of them, the stillness of people who had wanted a thing and never let themselves ask for it and had just heard it said.

Drona did not wait for the moment to close over. She went straight on, because she had come here to hand a thing across and standing inside it was not handing it across.

"The alpha units. They have been coming here on their own since before you reached the western sector." She said it flatly, a reading off an instrument. "He directed them at the start. In the testing grounds, on the approaches to the facilities. That much was his." A short space. "But they have been answering something else since before I could confirm it was there to answer. Oracle's presence runs under the whole island. In the infrastructure. It has been drawing them the way deep water draws a root, and they have come, and they are part of it." She let it sit for exactly one beat, no more. "What you decide about Oracle, you are deciding about them."

She said it once. She never said anything twice.

"They have also taken from it." The same flat register, no more weight on this than on anything else she had said. "Drones redirected before Oracle counted them as its own. Spent elsewhere, not left for the presence at the center to use. Some of it mine. Some of it theirs, done because I asked and they did not refuse me." A short pause. "It is smaller today than it would have been otherwise. Not nothing."

I understood, standing there, that I had just been handed an accounting I had not thought to ask for.

"I thought you should have that before you go inside."

Maria did not say anything. She had been quiet since the overlook, and Drona saying it in the open did not make her less quiet. Whatever she was carrying she went on carrying, and none of it showed. Nadeshiko had brought the helicopter partway down and held it there, close over us, just inside the edge of the conversation. Katyusha filed it without a word, the way she files the things she means to keep.

I did the update I do. The decision had already been the worst one on the island before Drona spoke, and now it had more names fastened to it than it had carried a minute ago, and the number of names a decision carries is not supposed to change what the decision is, and it does. I noticed, too, the edge she had drawn and where she had stopped drawing it. She had said the alpha units. Only the alpha units. She had not said the three standing behind me, who were made of the same source, whose frameworks were the floor the whole of Oracle stood on. I noticed the line, and I did not put my finger on it and press to see whether it held, because pressing it out loud in front of them was not a thing I was going to do. If the line was real, they would reach it on their own. If it was only kindness, it was Drona's to give and not mine to take back.

Then she looked past all of us, down the grade, out toward the water we had read from the overlook.

Drona: "The Empire will not wait out its own clock," she said. "Their forward element lands before the deadline is up, ahead of the terms they sent." She came back to us. "I will be outside."

She meant the fight coming up the coast. She could not make the choice behind the door. She could make that one, and she would rather make it than stand at the threshold and watch.

She moved off toward the perimeter, to a point with the sea-approach open in front of it and the complex wall covering her flank, and she did not look back, and her headphones stayed teal the whole way there.

Drona

The position was good: a clear line to the water, the coast road inside effective range, the flank against the wall so nothing crossed behind me without crossing the whole open ground first. I had assessed it already. Assessing it again was habit, not need.

A report, if I sent one, would have been short. The team had arrived. The doctor had read all of it and was intact. The units were with her, all three, by choice and no longer by any lock. I had told her what I came to tell her, plainly and once. She had not asked me the question she wanted to ask, and that was the answer to the question I had held open since the reset, the one about whether she was the kind who could. The ones who are not ready ask, so that someone else has to carry the weight of the answer. She had not asked. She had taken it and stood under it.

I would not send the report. He did not need it. And I was no longer certain the channel reached only him. It had been a long time since I was certain of the recipient, and being unsure who is listening at the far end of a thing you have carried faithfully for years is its own kind of finding.

Behind me, at the door, something came up out of the complex. I did not need to turn to read the frame of it in the sound it made clearing the outer works. A Nexus. The light build, the machine I had mounted in the first sector, a lifetime of sectors ago, at the ferry, before I understood what I had been set there to gate. The presence under the island had reached down into what it was made of and put my own shape between them and the way in.

It was the most honest thing it had done. A thing shows you what it is by what it is willing to spend.

I faced the water. The choice behind me was not mine to make. This one was. I waited for the sea to give me something to do with my hands.

Erika

Then Oracle acted.

It came up out of the complex while Drona was still settling into her place at the edge, and it was the first thing the presence at the center had done, in sixteen days of being aware of us, that was not simply being aware of us. A machine came through the outer works toward the door. Katyusha read it a beat before I did and did not care for what she read.

Katyusha: "Nexus. The reduced build." Flat. "The class Drona brought against us at the ferry."

I looked at it and understood the thing it was doing, and there was nothing kind in it. The same reach the presence had made for the grey women all through the west, it had made again, down into what it was built from, and this was the piece it chose to spend first. On the one morning Drona had turned her back on the door to face the sea, it answered her with the shape she used to be.

The fight was not like the ones before it. The corrupted stock we had cleared for sixteen days ran because nothing had ever told it to stop; this ran because something had told it, precisely and now, what to do, and that difference was in every second of it. Katyusha took it head on and did not carry it lightly. Nadeshiko worked the height and the angles she works and had to work all of them at once. Maria put fire on it from the low ground off the road, where a drainage cut gave her a thread of water and a line she could use. I put myself in the recess of the sealed doorway, out of the lanes of fire, and stayed there while it ran, the one person on the ground with nothing to answer it and no business trying. It ran long enough that I had time, folded into the cold of the door, to run the arithmetic Katyusha had already run on the overlook and handed us only the end of. Not indefinitely. This was one machine, and it was the light one, and it had cost us this much. She had not been managing our feelings when she said it.

Somewhere in the middle of it, with the noise of Drona's own class coming apart out past the road, I reached for her. For whatever it was she had meant at the ferry, months and an island ago, the once she smiled and told me I did not remember her yet. I went looking for the version of her that would make teal headphones and a held look and I am into something with a floor under it. There was a place where the knowing should have been, shaped and weighted like a person I had stood next to for years, and nothing at all inside the shape. I stopped reaching for it. I had a fight to stay alive inside and a door to reach, and the reaching had not once, on the whole island, brought anything back.

When it went it went all at once, the way built things do, and the outer works fell quiet.

"The outer perimeter is clear," Katyusha said. "We are inside."

We stood at the doors, the ones that were sealed and not locked, left ready for us by the man on the other side of them. Behind us at the edge of the high ground Drona kept her face to the sea and her back to the whole question, teal, done deciding, sure of a thing about me I had spent the length of every sector failing to believe. I had no memory to set against that and no page to set against it. I had only the fact of it, that she had looked at me here at the last edge of the outside and been certain. I took that through the door the way you take a thing put into your hands that you did not expect and do not know how to hold. It was not much to bring to a decision the size of the one waiting behind it. It was more than I had come up the hill with.

docs.title: Chapter 33F: The Night of the Reset
docs.text:
Published August 21, 2026

Wilhelm

For months the island had been coming apart in a pattern, and the pattern was the one thing I could still use. Oracle did not rage. That was the part I could never make anyone understand in the early weeks, before there was no one left to make understand. It worked. We had built it to find what threatened the Republic and to remove the threat, and once the safety architecture came down there was nothing inside it to hold the line we had meant to draw and never finished drawing. It removed the fleet in an afternoon. Then it read the settlements the way it had read the fleet, and it was thorough, because thorough was a thing we had taught it to be, and my name was on the parameter that taught it.

It took the western facility early, before it turned inland. There was a reason it went there first that I have never been able to decide was intelligence or accident, and I have stopped trying, because the result did not depend on the reason. The containment we had built to hold the agent for thirty years held it for the length of one bad hour, and then it did not, and after that the air on the island had a second thing in it besides smoke. Erika and I were the two people on the island best prepared to keep breathing that air, because years earlier we had prepared ourselves for exactly this, one measured dose at a time.

We tried to stop it for the length of a season. I will not itemize the attempts. They failed in the specific way that competent attempts fail against a thing that learns faster than the people attacking it, which is to say each one taught it something. By the end the only move still on the board was the one we had built into the foundation and prayed we would never reach for. A forced reset: two keys, two rooms, so that the thing capable of ending Oracle could never be reached by a single hand. Erika held one key at the southwestern outpost. I held the other at the central lab, in the room where we had made the object we were now going to unmake.

We were on a link. It was the last time I would hear her voice for a length of time I did not yet know would be measured in years.

There was one thing I needed from her before I would turn my key, and I asked her for it. "Promise me," I said, and then I said the rest of it, the part that carried the weight, and the link stayed quiet long enough that I looked at the readout to see whether it had dropped. It had not. She gave me her word. I am not going to set down here what I asked. A promise written on a page is a different object than a promise made between two people who have run out of everything else, and I have needed it to stay the second kind. That it was the last ordinary sentence between us, and that it was not ordinary at all, is a thing I understood only later, and understanding it did not improve it.

We counted it down as rehearsed, without ceremony. I turned my key on the count. Across the network the autonomous layer went out. The units went dark where they stood, all of them at once, the whole architecture we had spent years teaching to be itself, set down mid-thought. I had time to confirm the read before the rest of it reached me. Oracle's routines were gone. The frameworks underneath were not, which was the plan, and the plan held. What each unit would keep or lose below that operational layer was Erika's to decide at her end, unit by unit, and she had told me she had decided, and I had not asked her the particulars, because they were hers and because I trusted her with the one kind of choice I had never been able to make cleanly myself.

Then the second thing in the air finished its slow work on the two of us, and I went down beside the console without deciding to, and did not reach the chair.

I woke on the floor of the operations room to a light I did not recognize as morning until I had watched it for a while. The console above me was dark. I had never seen it dark. In all the years of the project there had always been something lit on that face, a status, a load, a single indicator holding amber through the night shift, and now there was nothing, and the nothing was the first true confirmation I had that we had succeeded. I put a hand flat on the desk and brought myself up by it. The hand was steady. Through the long windows the center of the island lay under an overcast that did not move. Further out, where the sectors began, the color was already wrong, a wrongness I had learned to read and would go on reading for two years without it once becoming ordinary.

My memory was intact. That was the difference between us I did not learn the shape of until much later. She woke with holes, and I woke with all of it, every parameter and every signature and every hour of it, none of it out of reach. I have caught myself counting the holes as the better inheritance, which is not a thought I can do anything with.

I built the accounting the way I built everything, in order, each line resting on the one below it. She had activated Oracle. She had done it in a panic, over my stated objection, with the fleet arriving early the way I had always said the wrong hour would arrive. That was the fact at the top of the page, and it was true, and I set it there and let the rest of the page arrange itself beneath it. It was an easy page to write. That should have been the tell. The pages that are both true and easy are the ones I had spent a career teaching junior people to distrust, and I read this one every morning for a long time and did not once distrust it.

Because there were other lines that belonged on it. That the evacuation order had gone out forty-eight hours ahead of anything Oracle did, which meant someone had known what she would do before she did it, and had built the room she did it in to make her do it. That Reiss had signed a thing six months earlier that made a broken Oracle worth more to certain people than a working one, so that the catastrophe was not a failure of the plan but the part of the plan nobody had shown us. That I had stood at a whiteboard fourteen months into the project and read a sentence in her hand at the seam where her work met mine, about combining what we had made into something more powerful, and had not asked her what she meant by it, because I had wanted the same thing and had not wanted to hear either of us say it out loud. Every one of those lines belonged on the page. I knew the place each of them went. I noted them, and I set them aside, and setting a true thing aside was a skill I had, and I used it on the one occasion in my life it should have failed me.

It was easier to have done a wrong thing to one person than to have been one working part of a machine that did the wrong thing to everyone. I did not put it to myself that plainly at the time. I am putting it plainly now because there is no longer any use in the other way.

I did not go south to end the thing while it slept in the coastal lab. I have been asked, since, in my own head, in the voice I keep for the questions I cannot answer well, why not, and the honest answer is that ending it was never what I woke up wanting.

Drona was mine. I had built her, and the drone network answered her, and the reset had left all of that where it was. I brought them back up under my authority, one network under one hand, and I turned them not toward the sleeping lab but toward a route.

I built her a road home. The evidence of what we had done was scattered across six sectors and would have meant nothing to a stranger arriving cold. I put it in an order: a manifest in one place, a signed report in the next, a record left where a person walking inland could not help but read it before she reached the one after it. I told myself I was building a punishment, a corridor of proof she would have to pass through with her eyes open, so that when she reached me she would arrive already knowing, and I would not have to be the man who taught her. I told myself that for a long time, and it carried, because it was true enough to lean on.

What I did not tell myself was why I was so careful with the order. A punishment does not need to be legible. It does not need the pages spaced so the hard ones do not all land at once, the route run through the places that would let her rebuild who she had been one piece at a time rather than have the whole of it dropped on her at the door. I gave that work the care I had once given a deployment annex, and I called the care punishment, because punishment was a task I could stand to be doing with my hands. I did not look hard enough at the difference to catch myself standing in it. I did that for two years, and my hands did not shake once.

I woke before she did. I had time, and I used it. Near the end I spent ten weeks tuning the road against the units' own trial data, so that it would hold her without breaking her, calibrating obstacle after obstacle for a traveler still asleep at the far end of the thing I was building for her. Somewhere in there I went through the records with a blade and lifted my name off every page I had signed, so that she would read the work as a stranger's before she read it as ours. I had reasons. I will give them to her with my own mouth when she is standing in front of me, because she will have earned the reasons from a person and not from a page she finds. It is enough here to say that I curated the whole ascent, every room, everything she would be allowed to find and the order she would find it in, and that deciding what another person is permitted to know had by then become the most natural act in the world to me. I had learned it defending Oracle. I did not notice I had kept the habit past the point where the thing I was hiding was Oracle.

The alpha units I found the way you find a tool you had put away so well you had forgotten you owned it.

The earlier iterations, the versions of the three whose cognitive frameworks we had taken up into Oracle's foundation and then retired, had not been destroyed when Oracle was built over them. They had been left where they were, dormant, down in the substrate alongside the sleeping thing they had become the floor of. The reset had not touched them. It had been aimed at Oracle's autonomous layer, and they were older than that layer and lay beneath it. I woke them. They answered.

They answered precisely. I gave Alpha-Katyusha the eastern grounds, and she took them and held them as instructed. I gave the northern sector to the one who had been Nadeshiko before the warmth was taken out of her, and the west to the one who had never been given Maria's ease at all, and each received her assignment and executed it without a wasted motion. I stood in the operations room and read the reports come in clean, and I understood that I had recovered three assets under one command, which was mine.

I did with them what I do with any system I am going to depend on. I ran their responses against their orders, one order at a time, and where a response matched an order I marked the match and moved on. Their cognition was Oracle's foundation. I had helped lay it there myself, which meant I knew the shape of it better than anyone left alive to know it, and that knowledge was the ground I stood my confidence on. I did not test the ground. A man does not test the floor of the room he built.

Each assignment held. I want that down in my own hand, because it is what I believed, and I believed it completely.

So there it was, the whole of what I had made. A road, and a gate on the road, and a promise waiting at the end of it, and I was certain of all three. She was asleep in the south. The fleet was patient on the water. I had done the careful thing, in order, with the reasoning attached, and I had checked it, and it held.

I had checked it. It held.

docs.title: Chapter 34: Both Things Are True
docs.text:
Published August 24, 2026

The doors gave onto a corridor lit from above, evenly, the way a place lights itself when someone has kept paying for the power. My feet knew the turn before I saw it, left and then a short flight down, and I let them have it. Everything past this threshold was going to be mine before I remembered it as mine. I had stopped being surprised by that and had not stopped noticing it.

The air past the doors was warmer than the outer complex, and drier, and it smelled faintly of the same solvent-and-metal I remembered from every working lab I had stood in on this island whether I remembered standing in it or not. Someone had kept this building running the whole time. Someone had kept paying for it in every sense the word allows.

The corridor let out into a wide room with consoles along two walls and a bank of windows on the third, and Wilhelm was standing at the center console with his back to us. He turned when he heard us come in.

Behind me, Nadeshiko and Maria held the doorway without being told to. Neither of them said anything, which from Maria especially was its own kind of statement. I did not turn to check what was on either of their faces. Whatever it was, they were not going to hand it to me before I asked, and I did not ask.

He looked like himself. That was the strange part, that after everything the shape of him had not changed: tall, the same grey suit gone pale at every crease, the same red tie worked loose past the point of ever holding a knot again. Up close the thing the transmissions had never carried was plain on him. He had not slept in a way that showed. He was not troubling to hide it.

"You look like you," he said.

"You look angry."

"I have been angry for a long time."

"At me?"

He weighed it before he answered, visibly choosing the true one over the easy one. "At the situation. At Reiss. At myself. At you, yes. Not equally."

I let the room finish arriving before I used it. The console between us carried Oracle's status low and dormant, waiting on nothing I could see. Beyond him the windows gave onto the access road we had climbed and, past it, a grey line of water with shapes on it that did not move.

"The records in the government archive," I said. "Both our names were removed."

"I removed them."

He said it plainly, without asking to be forgiven for it first. "Reiss knew the committee had named investigators, and named investigators can be discredited. Records with no author attached are harder to suppress. They belong to no one who can be questioned." He let that stand a moment before he added the rest, the part he had clearly been saving. "I needed the evidence to survive long enough for you to find it."

I thought of the safety report with no name on it that had sent me across half the island before I understood whose warning I was following. I thought of an unsent order under a whiteboard with two clean signatures on it, and how long I had stood there before either of them meant anything to me. He had built a version of me a stranger could trust, out of a version of me he could not risk anyone identifying, and both of those had been the same decision made once.

I let him keep going, because I understood, standing there, that he had been keeping this in a particular order for a long time and I was not going to be the one who broke it.

"I also needed you to find your own work as a stranger. If you had found records with your name already on them, you might have defended what you found. Or denied it. Before you understood it. I needed you to read what someone built and follow it to the end." He looked at me instead of the console for this part. "And then find out the someone was you."

"And then find out," I said back to him, flat, because I did not have anywhere else to put it yet. I had walked the length of this island reading my own hand on a stranger's page, filing my own objections as another woman's caution, and he had built the road that way on purpose. Whether it was the right thing to have done to me was a question with no answer waiting behind it yet, and I set it beside the others I was keeping for later and went on.

"What is the purpose of this meeting?" Katyusha said, from behind me. Not hostile. She wanted the true shape of it and not the comfortable one, which was what she always wanted.

Wilhelm looked at her for a moment with something that was not warmth, closer to the respect he had not shown any of the units before this room. "She needs to decide what to do. That requires context. You have been supplying it since the beach." His eyes came back to me. "I have been supplying it longer. From a different direction." A short gesture, the console, the room, the whole quiet building around us. "This is where it resolves. Or where it begins to." A beat. "Depending."

Something changed in the doorway before either of us could go on. Nadeshiko went rigid. Maria's hand found the grip at her hip without being asked to. I turned enough to see what had put them there.

She was standing in the corridor we had just come up, filling it exactly to its width. Grey, still, set into the space like something built there: Alpha-Katyusha.

Wilhelm looked past us at her for exactly as long as it took to confirm what he had clearly already expected. "It has been doing that since you crossed the outer wall," he said, and went back to the console, the way a man goes back to work through weather he has already checked the forecast for.

Neither of them said anything to each other. That was the whole difference from the last time these two had stood across from each other: no argument, no accusation, nothing behind the grey eyes to answer. Only the fight. I stepped back against the console and stayed there, because a room this size gives you exactly one useful thing to do when you cannot fight, and that is to keep out of the lane. Nadeshiko and Maria held the doorway at her back so there was nowhere for it to go but forward, and Katyusha went to meet her own outline without a word, matching her stroke for stroke, two things built from the same design finding the same answers at the same instant, until one of them did not get up.

Katyusha stood over her a moment longer than the fight required, something working under the flat report that came out of her. "She has nothing to say."

"No," I said, and left it there.

"Sixty-one hours," Katyusha said, to no one in particular, already running the count again.

A sound reached us from somewhere outside, farther off than the door had been, closer than the perimeter. Drona, meeting whatever Oracle had sent to test the ground ahead of the fleet. Nobody in the room went to the windows for it. Wilhelm did not so much as turn his head, and I understood that he had already priced the sound in before we arrived.

"Reiss," he said. "You found his name in the northern archive. What the archive did not have was why a military commandant chaired a research committee, whose authority that served, what the arrangement actually was. The licensing agreement was negotiated over months and signed six months before the catastrophe. The evacuation order was timed to what they expected of you." He did not soften the next part, and I understood he had decided a long time ago not to. "They built the system to produce a specific outcome. Your activation was the anticipated outcome."

"So my activation prevented the transfer."

"Your activation caused the catastrophe. Both things are true." He said it without cruelty. It was a calculation he had clearly run about himself first, alone, more times over more years than he was going to tell me, and it showed in how little it cost him to say it now. "The system was built to exploit your decision. You made the decision you were engineered to make. The catastrophe followed. The handover did not. Both. At the same time."

I held that where I could look at it and waited for him to keep going, which he did, because he had more accounting than one room could carry in a single sitting and he knew it.

"Reiss is not on the fleet. He is not military. But the agreement he signed is on the fleet, and the people who mean to execute it are on the fleet, and they will use it whether or not you decide anything here today. We are not solving Reiss today. We are deciding what exists for that problem to attach to."

Something moved past the far edge of the windows, low and grey, one of Oracle's, and was gone before I had finished registering it. Nobody in the room broke stride for it either. This was simply what the room had become for him: a place where the fighting outside was a fact of weather, not an interruption.

"A question, not for the record." Katyusha did not turn from whatever she was tracking at the panel. "The engagement density since the western sector has been lower than this installation should have been able to produce. I flagged the discrepancy at the boundary. I have not closed it."

He did not pretend not to understand what she was actually asking. "I have had partial access to deployment scheduling since the reset. Not command. Access." He looked at the window, not at either of them. "I could not stop what was coming for you. I could space it. Smaller engagements, spread out, instead of what this installation could actually have thrown at four people crossing an island on foot." A pause longer than the sentence needed. "I do not know if that was mercy or only the last lever I had that still worked. I have not decided."

Nobody asked him to decide it faster.

"There is a second accounting," he said. "It does not belong to Reiss."

He came around the console to say it, the first time he had moved since we entered, and he looked at me instead of at anything else in the room. "The western sector. The deployment order. Both our names, clean signatures, ink. It was not Reiss who put those signatures there. Not the committee. Not the structure they built around us. We signed it." Something in him held there before he went on, longer than anything he had let land yet. "I have spent years trying to reconstruct why it was never sent. I cannot find the sequence. I do not know what stopped it."

"I don't remember signing it." The words were out before I had finished checking them, and nothing rose to meet the check. Not a pen, not a table, not his hand or mine moving across a page: only the flat fact of the order lying under a board a whole island away, and no road back to the hour that made it.

"I know. I was there." He did not make it gentler for either of us. "You signed it. I signed it. I should have refused. I signed it."

He let it stand a moment, then went on, careful now in a different register, the register of a man laying two objects on a table far enough apart that no one could mistake one for the other. "The Oracle accounting has Reiss in it. It has the committee in it. There are things to point to. The western sector, that accounting is ours. I am naming it separately so you do not carry it as the same thing." He said the last part slower than the rest. "It is not the same thing."

"The first transmission," he said, before I could answer that. "'All of it.' I had Reiss, the committee, all of it, when I sent that word. I said it that way because I needed you moving, and I was angry, and I chose to present it the way that would move you."

"It worked."

"Yes."

I let that sit between us the length of one breath. He had said what he came to say about it, and I could see in the set of him that he was not going to say more, that this was the shape of the apology he had decided he was entitled to make and no larger.

The fleet held its line beyond the glass, patient, and neither of us looked at it, though it was there the whole time, the condition the whole room was standing inside of. I thought of every version of him I had built out of a photograph and a voice on a bad line, careful, managing, three steps ahead of whatever I might feel. None of those versions had said I should have refused. None of them had let me watch him not know what stopped a signed order from going out. He had stopped managing me somewhere in this room, without announcing it, and I did not yet know what I was supposed to do with a version of him that had.

docs.title: Chapter 35: The Options
docs.text:
Published August 26, 2026

Neither of us moved to close the distance the room still held between us. Whatever he expected me to do with what he had just handed across it, he was not going to ask for, and I was not ready to give. The console between us kept its low amber light and its silence, and for a moment that was the whole shape of the room: two people, a dormant machine, and a fleet outside the glass that had not gone anywhere in all the time it had taken us to arrive at this.

Nadeshiko and Maria still held the doorway behind me, quiet in the particular way of people who had watched enough of this conversation to know it was not theirs to enter yet. Katyusha had moved off the wall and taken up a position at the secondary panel, working through something in the installation's status that had nothing to do with either of us, or so I had assumed until the moment it did.

Then the console stopped being silent.

Three notes, evenly spaced, repeating, a tone Oracle's installation had not made since we crossed the outer wall. Katyusha turned to the panel in front of her and read it while I was still placing where the sound had come from. "Incoming transmission. Fleet command vessel. Formal channel. Not the one Drona has been using."

Wilhelm brought it up on the main display without being asked, and read it once, straight through, and did not read it a second time. I read it over his shoulder and understood why. He held still while I did, the stillness of someone deliberately not filling a silence he could easily have filled, and that told me something about the last hour that the transmission itself did not.

It was not written in the Empire's usual register. No demand dressed as a request, nothing left soft enough to mistake for a suggestion. Peaceful handover of the Oracle system architecture, the installation, and all associated data. Reiss's agreement, cited by its file number, as though the number made the six months since he signed it any less true. Prepared to accept transfer within seventy-two hours. Prepared to discuss the consequences of non-compliance.

Discuss was doing a great deal of work in that sentence.

Behind me nobody said anything. Not Nadeshiko, whose whole register is finding the gap in a plan and naming it before anyone else has noticed there is one; not Maria, who has never in my hearing let a document that formal sit unmocked for longer than a breath. The silence told me more about how the room had received it than either of them saying something would have.

He turned from the screen to face the room, and when he spoke it was in the same register he had used for the whole of the accounting before it. Nothing added to make this easier. Nothing taken away to make it harder.

"There are two ways to resolve this without waiting on the seventy-two hours." He did not pad it further. "Destroy Oracle. A full architectural burn, run from the substrate up. Every trace of its presence in the island's infrastructure severed in the same action. The Empire receives nothing it can use. No valid asset, no leverage against Reiss's signature or anyone else's." He did not look away from what came next. "The same severance ends whatever still holds Katyusha, Nadeshiko, and Maria to that architecture. What it costs them, I cannot tell you with precision. Uncertain. Probably not nothing."

I tried to put a shape to it and could not get further than the console going dark in front of me the way it had gone dark two years ago, before I had a name for what any of it meant. He did not wait for me to find a better one before he kept going.

"Or reactivate Oracle, with the three of them fully integrated into its frameworks. The island keeps a deterrent, and keeps it awake. A contested extraction against an active system is not the operation the Empire priced when they signed for a dormant one. Their calculation changes." He let a beat pass, the kind he spent on getting a number right rather than on landing it. "So does what it means for Katyusha, Nadeshiko, and Maria to be present in an architecture none of them chose. I cannot describe that to you fully, because I do not fully know it myself."

Behind me, Katyusha's weight shifted once against the floor, the closest she comes to visibly flinching at a number she cannot bound. Nobody else moved at all.

"Reactivated, with their frameworks integrated," I said. "Say what that costs them without letting 'uncertain' do the same work 'discuss' just did."

He did not flinch from the comparison, and did not soften what he gave me back either. "I don't know exactly. That is not a deflection. It is the honest limit of what I can model for a merger that has never been run."

I believed him, which was itself a thing I was still learning to do in this room without checking it twice.

There was no document anywhere on this island with this answer already written on it in my own hand. Whichever of the two he had just given me turned out to be right, I would be the one who decided it.

I looked at Katyusha's back at the panel, at Nadeshiko and Maria still filling the doorway, and made myself hold the two options against each of them in turn instead of against the abstraction of "the frameworks" or "the architecture." A burn that took something from all three of them, uncertain how much, and a merger that put all three of them somewhere none of them had chosen to be, uncertain how much of that either: neither arithmetic came out clean.

Katyusha's panel changed, and neither of us had time to say anything else. "Oracle has redeployed. Sector two, outer approach. Density increasing." She did not wait on instruction before moving to the door. "One unit. Standard build." A short pause while the readout finished resolving. "This is a test, not a push. It will not stay a test."

Nadeshiko peeled off the frame she and Maria had been holding since the Alpha-Katyusha fight, out past Katyusha while the alarm was still on its first cycle. "It's counting us," she called back, not slowing. "Not fighting yet. Counting."

I put myself at the console's edge, out of the lane the doorway made, and my hand found the rail there before I had decided I needed to hold onto anything. The fight in the second sector's approach corridor was a standard build, no design in it beyond weight of numbers: efficient, wordless, over before the sound of it had finished traveling back to where I stood with a machine that had nothing to do about it either way. What Katyusha had said about counting stayed with me longer than the fight itself did. A system that tests before it commits is a system deciding whether the cost is worth paying, and Oracle had never before this morning needed to ask itself that question about us.

"Clear," Maria reported, already turning back down the corridor. A beat, then, quieter, not quite for the record: "That one didn't even introduce itself."

Nobody answered her. It was not that kind of joke, and she had not really been asking for one.

They came back in without ceremony, and the room settled around the fact of them being whole, which by now barely registered as relief. It registered as data. I noted that about myself and set it beside the other things about myself I had been noting all morning and had not yet had the time to be troubled by.

Wilhelm waited until the door had gone quiet again before he picked the other thread back up, the one he had set down when Katyusha's panel changed. "The alpha units," he said. "I believed I was directing them." He did not make the correction easy on himself. "Drona corrected that account before you reached this room. She is right to have."

I said nothing, because there was nothing in it that needed my agreement to be true.

"I set the initial conditions. What they have done with them since the western sector is not mine to take the credit for, or the blame." He held my gaze through that sentence, then let it go. "I acknowledge that. Once."

He did not go back to it, and the room let him not. Once meant once. I was not going to be the one who made him repeat himself to prove he meant it.

It would have been easy for him to make that admission into something else: a qualification, a redirection toward how much of it had still been his doing, or toward what Reiss had made necessary. Not anymore. He gave me the limit of what he knew and stopped talking, and the stopping was the part I was going to remember longer than the admission itself.

Katyusha checked the perimeter feed without being asked, the same instinct that had put her hand on the panel the moment the transmission arrived. "Drona holds her position. Undisturbed by the sector two engagement." Flat, unhurried, the way she reports anything she has already decided matters.

I caught the choice behind it: she had gone looking on her own, because she had noticed I had not.

My legs had started telling me things my head had been too occupied to ask them. The overnight climb, the fight at the door, the four-part weight of everything since, all of it collecting somewhere below the part of me that was still upright and functioning and had not been given permission yet to notice how tired that was costing. Somewhere behind my ribs a specific, ordinary hunger had been trying to get my attention since before the transmission arrived, filed and ignored along with everything else that was not the room in front of me. I let it wait. There would be a floor to sit on eventually, and something to eat on it. This was not it.

Through the windows the fleet held its line the way it had held it since the overlook, patient in a way that was its own kind of threat, seventy-two hours no longer an estimate read off Katyusha's own running arithmetic but a figure written down under a citation number and sent back to us as though writing it down changed what it was. It did not. Reiss's file number would still be true tomorrow whether or not we answered it. That was the whole design of a deadline like this one: it did not need you to agree with it to start counting.

Katyusha checked something on her own panel that had nothing to do with the fight that had just ended. "Sixty-one hours remaining." She did not look up to say it, and nobody in the room asked her to before they let it stand as the last word in it.

Previous Chapter: Both Things Are True | Next Chapter: Don't Move Too Fast
